title: The Metamorphosis, Kafka
subject: litterature
description: Gregor Samsa wakes up turned into an insect. Kafka shows how a family, and a whole society, reject the person who can no longer work.

hero.hook: One morning Gregor Samsa wakes up transformed: the sentence that sums up an entire age.

blocks.text: Published in **1915**, [[The Metamorphosis]] opens with one of the most famous first lines in literature: “As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams, he found himself changed into a monstrous insect.” The original German title is *Die Verwandlung*. **Franz Kafka**, who was born in **1883** and died in **1924**, is not writing a fantasy tale here. He is writing the model case of modern dehumanization.

Written in record time in November **1912**, the story explores what happens when a person stops being productive. He instantly loses his standing as a human being in the eyes of his own family. The absurd transformation only reveals an alienation that was already at work before his body changed.

sections.title: The making of a masterpiece of the absurd

blocks.text: Kafka wrote the novella in **1912**, during a burst of creative energy in Prague. He treats the transformation with **clinical realism**: no supernatural explanation, no search for a cause. All the attention goes to the practical and family consequences.

blocks.caption: Gregor's transformation: Kafka banned any picture of the insect on the cover

blocks.text: Kafka strictly forbade his publisher to draw the insect on the cover. He wanted every reader to imagine his own version of the horror.

His friend [[Max Brod]] disobeyed Kafka's last wishes. Kafka had asked for his manuscripts to be destroyed. Brod published them after his death, and so saved a body of work that became [[Kafkaesque]] in the purest sense. The adjective describes a situation that is absurd, crushing, and beyond all logic.

Before his transformation, **Gregor Samsa** is a **traveling salesman**, a commercial agent always on the road. He is the only source of money in his family. His life is a chain of exhausting trips and obedience to a tyrannical boss. He secretly dreams of quitting, but the family debt keeps him in place.

By becoming a piece of “vermin,” Gregor makes visible a dehumanization that was already there. The German word *Ungeziefer* means an unclean animal, unwanted, worth nothing. Oddly enough, this monstrous shape finally frees him from the 5 a.m. train: he no longer has to leave for work.

At first his sister **Grete** feeds Gregor and cleans his room with real devotion. But time wears that solidarity down. To survive, every member of the family goes back to work: the father finds a job, the mother sews, Grete becomes a shop assistant. Gregor turns into a shameful burden.

The Samsas rent rooms to [[boarders]], lodgers who also take their meals in the house. Gregor is reduced to living out of sight. When Grete announces that they have to “get rid of him,” Gregor lets himself starve. He understands that there is no place left for him in a family that has become “normal” again.

sections.title: The survivors and the end of the nightmare

blocks.text: Gregor's death is not a tragedy for the family. It is a **release**. They take a tram ride out of town, already thinking about Grete's marriage. Within a few weeks Gregor is wiped out of their memory. The return to ordinary life turns out to be more frightening than the metamorphosis itself.

blocks.caption: Prague in the early 20th century: the city where Kafka wrote his novella

blocks.text: The novella shows how work and family life crush a person as soon as he stops being economically useful. Kafka describes a bureaucratic world where a man is nothing but a function. Family love turns out to depend on productivity. The absurd part is not the metamorphosis. It is the reaction of those closest to him, who would rather erase the sick man than pity him.
[[The Metamorphosis]] uses the absurd change of a man into an insect to attack alienation through work and the fragility of bonds built on economic usefulness.
